turns.doctor_question: Hello, welcome in. What brings you to see me today?
turns.patient_response: Well, hi. Thank you for seeing me. I know it might sound a little silly, or maybe it's not a big deal, but honestly, what made me finally make the appointment is... well, it's work. I'm in advertising sales, and we have these really, really long sales strategy meetings. I mean, sometimes they go on for hours, and the expectation is very clearly that we all sit around the conference table, take notes, and pay attention. But I just... I can't seem to stay in my chair. I keep getting up. And I know I’m supposed to stay seated, it's so obvious that everyone else is just sitting there fine, but I find myself making excuses to get up, even if it’s just to refill my water bottle for the third time, or I'll go pace by the printer pretending I'm waiting for a document that isn't even printing yet. It's just this constant need to not be sitting, and it's starting to feel really noticeable, you know? Like my boss gave me a look last Tuesday when I got up during the Q3 projections, and I just thought, 'Okay, I need to figure out why I can't just sit still like a normal person during a meeting.'

symptom_reasoning.S011: The patient explicitly states they keep getting up and leaving their chair during long meetings where they are expected to stay seated.
symptom_reasoning.S012: The patient describes a 'constant need to not be sitting' and an inability to 'just sit still,' which indicates a strong feeling of restlessness.

turns.doctor_question: Looking back to your childhood and school years, did you have similar difficulties sitting still?
turns.patient_response:
Oh, gosh, yes. I mean... yes, absolutely. It’s actually funny you ask that, because I was just talking to my mom about this a little while ago, and... well, I remember this starting way, way before high school. Like, early elementary school. 

My mom actually kept all my old report cards in this big yellow binder—she's very organized, which is ironic, because I am definitely not—and if you look back at what my teachers wrote, it’s honestly like reading a broken record. Every single year, Mrs. Davis in second grade, Mr. Miller in fourth grade... they all wrote that I was "bright but rushed." That was the exact phrase they loved to use. Like I just couldn't slow down enough to finish anything properly, I was just constantly speeding through everything so I could go do something else. 

And I was always, always getting in trouble because I talked out of turn. I’d just blurt things out in the middle of a lesson because I felt like if I didn't say it right that exact second, I'd forget it, or like I just couldn't hold it in, you know? And the homework... oh, the homework was a nightmare. I would forget it constantly. Even if I actually sat down and did it, which was a whole ordeal in itself, I'd leave it on the kitchen table or completely forget to turn it in. 

And my desk at school... I don't know if you remember those old desks with the little cubby space inside? Mine was just... it was a complete disaster zone. Just absolutely stuffed to the brim with half-finished papers, crumpled up worksheets, broken pencils... I would literally have to shove things in and slam the top down before it all spilled out onto the floor. So, yeah, it's definitely not a new problem at all, it's been happening pretty much my whole life.

symptom_reasoning.S001: The patient describes being 'rushed' and 'speeding through everything,' which indicates a failure to give close attention to details.
symptom_reasoning.S004: The patient mentions having 'half-finished papers' and being unable to 'finish anything properly,' showing a failure to follow through and finish schoolwork.
symptom_reasoning.S005: The patient describes their school desk as a 'complete disaster zone' stuffed with papers, demonstrating difficulty organizing tasks and belongings.
symptom_reasoning.S009: The patient reports constantly forgetting their homework, leaving it at home, or forgetting to turn it in.
symptom_reasoning.S016: The patient explicitly states they would 'talk out of turn' and 'blurt things out in the middle of a lesson.'

turns.doctor_question: Aside from trouble sitting still, do you currently struggle to sustain your focus or pay close attention to details when working on tasks?
turns.patient_response:
Oh, completely. It's so frustrating because... well, I really do try. Like, I'll go into one of those longer strategy meetings I mentioned—the ones that just drag on forever—and I'll literally tell myself beforehand, 'Okay, this time I'm going to lock in, I'm going to absorb everything, no distractions.' And I really do start out focused! For the first few minutes, I'm right there with them, looking at the presenter, nodding along, taking a note or two. 

But then... I don't even know how it happens, honestly. It’s like a switch just flips in my brain without me even noticing, and suddenly I'll snap back to reality and realize I've just been staring at the exact same PowerPoint slide for who knows how long, and I have absolutely no idea what the last point was. The presenter is on a completely different topic, and my mind is just blank. 

And it's not just in meetings, either, it happens when I'm alone at my desk, too. Like when I'm trying to read through a client brief. Client briefs are huge in advertising sales, you know, because if you miss a tiny detail about what the brand wants, it can completely derail the whole pitch and make us look really unprofessional. So I'll open the document, and I'll be reading, but after a few minutes, I'll catch myself just... looking at the same paragraph over and over again. My eyes are moving over the words, so physically I am reading, but nothing is actually registering in my brain. I'll have to go back and re-read the same section three, maybe four times just to figure out what they're actually asking for, because my mind was just completely somewhere else while I was supposedly reading it. It makes me so paranoid that I'm going to miss some crucial detail just because I spaced out while staring right at it.

symptom_reasoning.S001: The patient agrees ('Oh, completely') to struggling to pay close attention to details and expresses paranoia about missing crucial details in client briefs due to spacing out.
symptom_reasoning.S002: The patient describes a clear inability to sustain focus during long meetings and while reading documents, losing track of the content after just a few minutes.
symptom_reasoning.S059: The patient explicitly states that their 'mind is just blank' during meetings and describes severe difficulty concentrating on reading tasks, where nothing registers in their brain.
